title: CEO Interview: Chase Idleman of Arlow
author: Joel Trammell
summary: Trammell interviews Chase Idleman, who left two decades in medtech leadership to found Arlow, an AgeTech company pairing AI tools with human advisors to help older adults and their families. Idleman recounts growing up expecting to inherit his parents' air ambulance business, being urged out of the family nest, and starting Arlow after a midlife reckoning when that business was sold. Much of the conversation concerns the leadership transition from corporate to startup life: corporate work taught discipline and scale, but founding meant learning a new language of pitch decks and valuations and discovering that it is ten times harder than expected. He names initiative as the essential founder trait, describes waking at 3 a.m. with responsibility to investors and to employees who took a chance, and acknowledges the loneliness of the role. The second half explains the demographic case for Arlow, with 11,000 Americans turning 65 each day, and its employer-sold model aimed at the sandwich generation. Idleman closes with the question he asks his team daily about whether AI in the product actually makes someone's life easier.
points: Idleman credits his corporate years with the discipline and business fundamentals he relies on daily as a founder.
He says the core founder skill is initiative, since a startup offers no fences and no obvious direction to run.
He describes the anxiety of feeling responsible not only to investors but to employees who left secure jobs to join him.
Arlow is sold mainly through employers to reduce absenteeism among workers caring for aging parents, a benefit only 7% of employers offer.
He tests every AI feature by asking whether it genuinely makes a user's life easier or merely exists because it can.
quotes: Moving over to the startup side of things is hard. I told a friend this the other day: If you think you know it’s going to be hard, expect it to be 10 times harder than that.

I think people sometimes paint the corporate world in a really negative light compared to owning your own business. But the corporate world teaches you a lot of good things. It teaches you discipline.
You have to wake up and figure out which direction to go. You not only have to have the initiative to get out of bed, but you have to know which way to run.
They have made a big sacrifice to be here on this ship with us. So there is a different level of anxiety you have to navigate day to day.
I have a co-founder and she’s phenomenal, and I have a great team. I also have a circle of friends that I commiserate with, but it’s a very close circle.
Only 7% of employers offer any form of assistance for employees helping older adults at home.

If we’re using AI in our product, are we doing it just because we can, or are we using it to actually make someone’s life easier—to help them be more efficient, more organized, and get more accurate information?
